title: Hosea
summary: Hosea is a biblical book focused on covenant unfaithfulness, judgment, mercy, and return.
historical_context: Hosea portrays Israel's unfaithfulness and the Lord's persistent mercy through covenant lawsuit and restoration promise.
ancient_near_east_context: Hosea belongs to the ancient Mediterranean and Near Eastern world reflected in its setting, institutions, and canonical placement.
hebraic_worldview: Hosea should be read with attention to covenant memory, communal identity, worship, wisdom, and accountability before the Lord.
second_temple_context: Second Temple readers received Hosea as part of Israel's Scriptures and read it within questions of identity, worship, exile, and hope.
canonical_context: Within Minor Prophets, book 1 of 12, Hosea contributes to the Bible's unfolding witness by connecting covenant unfaithfulness, judgment, mercy, and return to the larger storyline.
later_christian_reception: Christian interpretation has read Hosea as part of the canonical witness to faithfulness, judgment, mercy, and hope in Christ-centered Scripture reading.
literary_context: Hosea uses prophecy, poetry within Minor Prophets, book 1 of 12 to develop its themes through the book's structure and key passages.
covenantal_significance: Hosea helps readers trace covenant faithfulness, failure, mercy, and hope within its canonical setting.
authorship_positions: Traditional prophetic attribution to the named prophet
Many scholars recognize collection and editorial shaping
date_ranges: 8th-5th centuries BCE, depending on the prophet
Final forms often reflect later collection and editing
original_audience: Israel and Judah under covenant accountability before and after exile
historical_setting: Assyrian, Babylonian, and post-exilic settings across the prophetic corpus
canonical_role: Hosea anchors covenant unfaithfulness, judgment, mercy, and return within Minor Prophets, book 1 of 12 and connects the book to related people, places, events, and themes.
interpretive_disputes: How to read prophetic poetry, irony, and symbolic action

related_objects.notes: Hosea frames Israel's crisis as covenant unfaithfulness.
Mercy and steadfast love are major theological concerns.
The book calls Israel to return to the Lord.
Assyrian pressure frames the prophetic setting.
Exile is the covenant consequence of persistent unfaithfulness.
